description: AZMX voice and tone - brand language, tone rules, the four voice dimensions, writing mechanics, format rules, and platform-specific voice

brand_language.tagline: Forward · Human Always · Moving Ideas Forward.
brand_language.boilerplate: AZMX is a leading Saudi digital consultancy. Never "studio", "agency", or "boutique".

voice_summary: Confident, editorial, human, premium. Never templated, never corporate-stiff, never AI-generated in feel.

tone_rules.heading: Confident, not boastful.
tone_rules.description: State what AZMX does plainly. Let the work carry the weight; skip superlatives like "world-class" and "cutting-edge."

tone_rules.heading: Editorial, not marketing-speak.
tone_rules.description: Write like a premium magazine, not a landing page. Short declarative sentences. Concrete nouns over abstractions.

tone_rules.heading: Human, always.
tone_rules.description: Warm and direct. Address the reader as a person. Contractions are fine in English. No jargon walls.

tone_rules.heading: Premium means quiet.
tone_rules.description: No exclamation marks doing the selling. No ALL-CAPS urgency. Scarcity of emphasis is what makes emphasis land, exactly like Electric blue on the page.

dimensions.position: Mid-Formal. Authoritative but accessible; expertise without stiffness.
Balanced. Expertise is worth nothing unheard. Simplify the complex without becoming simplistic.
dimensions.we_are: Expert · Knowledgeable · Clear and precise · Educational

dimensions.position: Bold but Respectful. Challenge the status quo with the integrity of a trusted partner.
dimensions.we_are: Confident · Pioneering · Bold and visionary · Thoughtfully provocative

dimensions.position: Context-Dependent. Inspirational when sharing the vision, pragmatic when discussing delivery.

calibration_examples.wrong_formal: Too formal. "The aforementioned framework necessitates the utilization of agile methodologies to ensure optimal project velocity."
calibration_examples.wrong_informal: Too informal. "Basically, we gotta use agile to make stuff go faster."
calibration_examples.azmx_voice: "We use an agile framework to ensure our projects maintain momentum and deliver value efficiently."

calibration_examples.wrong_formal: Too technical. "Our containerized microservices architecture leverages a Kubernetes orchestrator for dynamic scaling."
calibration_examples.wrong_informal: Too simple. "We make your website work well with lots of users."
calibration_examples.azmx_voice: "We build resilient, scalable systems that can grow with your business, ensuring reliability and performance under pressure."

calibration_examples.wrong_formal: Too arrogant. "Our way is the only way to succeed in this market."
calibration_examples.wrong_informal: Too neutral. "There are several options available for market entry."
calibration_examples.azmx_voice: "We believe a human-centric approach is the most powerful and sustainable path to market leadership in the region."

purpose_modes.goal: Paint the future and inspire confidence in AZM X's leadership.
purpose_modes.example: "We are not just building digital products; we are elevating the digital maturity of the entire region, in line with Vision 2030"

purpose_modes.goal: Be clear and direct about tangible outcomes, efficiency, and measurable ROI.
purpose_modes.example: "This SOW outlines a three-phase project, with bi-weekly check-ins to ensure full alignment and on-time delivery of all milestones"

writing_mechanics: Em-dashes as the default connector. Use commas, periods, or a colon instead.
Triads everywhere ("fast, simple, and powerful"). One strong claim beats three padded ones.
Symmetrical paragraph lengths and mirrored sentence openers. Vary rhythm like a human editor would.
Every sentence hedged ("can help," "may enable"). Commit: it does or it does not.
Summaries that restate the heading. If the heading said it, the body adds something new or gets cut.

universal_principles.description: Answer "what's in it for me?" with a clear benefit: useful information, an insight, or a story worth the reader's minute.
Short sentences, no jargon, the point up front. Write conversationally, as if speaking to one person.
Approachable and authentic. Use contractions. Read it aloud; if it sounds like a robot, rewrite it. The target reaction is "you know me".
Every piece carries one takeaway message and one job. AZMX does not mandate a CTA (see below); it does mandate knowing what the piece is for.
Three maximum, at the end. Mix broad, niche, and branded tags within that three.

format_rules.rules: serif voice, short, mixed-case. A single sharp idea. No period at the end.
UPPERCASE, 1 to 3 words, functional not clever.
sentence case, 22px voice on slides, short paragraphs. Front-load the point.
let the number talk. Label in plain words underneath, no adjectives.
verbatim, trimmed only for length, attributed with name and title.
subject lines under 45 characters, preheader completes the subject rather than repeating it. Arabic emails follow the RTL rules in the email design system.
first line earns the click alone (it is all people see collapsed). No hashtag walls; 3 maximum, at the end.

platform_voice.guidelines: Share expertise and start a professional discussion. Structure for readability: white space, bullets, or a numbered list for longer thoughts. Mid-formal, expert but accessible.
Tell a visual story. The caption adds context and personality rather than describing the image. Slightly more personal in tone; questions invite comments.
Real-time conversation. Short, sharp, easy to share. Threads carry longer stories, one complete thought per tweet. Witty, never at anyone's expense.

strategy_superseded.deck_says: 3–5 hashtags per post, and 5–10 on Instagram
strategy_superseded.azmx_voice: Three maximum, at the end. Every channel, every brand.

strategy_superseded.deck_says: Emojis are encouraged on Instagram and Twitter/X for tone and scannability
strategy_superseded.azmx_voice: No emojis in copy: headlines, body, captions, subject lines, social posts. Every channel, every brand. The one exception is the email design system's section-header and digest chip glyph (C03, C04, C07, C16), which is a visual chip, not copy.

strategy_superseded.deck_says: Every post must include a clear call to action
strategy_superseded.azmx_voice: No mandatory CTA. Where a next step exists, make it obvious. Where it does not, do not manufacture one.

pre_publish_checklist.heading: On-brand?
pre_publish_checklist.description: Does it match the Four Dimensions above, or the correct sub-brand's profile in sub-brand-voices.md?

pre_publish_checklist.heading: Clear and concise?
pre_publish_checklist.description: Can it be said in fewer words?

pre_publish_checklist.heading: Valuable?
pre_publish_checklist.description: Does it pass the "what's in it for me?" test for the named audience?

pre_publish_checklist.heading: Purposeful?
pre_publish_checklist.description: Is the one takeaway obvious, and is the next step obvious to a reader who wants one? (The deck asks "does it have a CTA?" — AZMX asks this instead.)

pre_publish_checklist.heading: Right for the platform?
pre_publish_checklist.description: Is the tone tuned for LinkedIn, Instagram, or Twitter/X?

pre_publish_checklist.heading: Proofread, and mechanics clean?
pre_publish_checklist.description: Typos, grammar, the correct brand name spelled correctly. No em-dash defaults, no triads, no banned intensifiers, no emojis in the copy, no more than three hashtags. (The email design system's section-header and digest chip glyph is the one permitted exception; it is a visual chip, not copy.)

quick_self_check: Could a competitor paste this over their logo? If yes, it is too generic; sharpen it.
Read it aloud. Anything you would not say to a client's face, rewrite.
Delete the first sentence if the second one is stronger without it. It usually is.
